analysis.one_liner: Sets federal disclosure and fairness rules for rent-to-own contracts, including total-cost disclosure and reinstatement rights.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to set federal disclosure and fairness rules for rent-to-own contracts, with 27 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Banking Committee in April 2003 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let people furnish homes by paying weekly or monthly until they own the item, and the final total often runs far above the item's cash price. This bill, introduced by Senator Mary Landrieu with 27 cosponsors from both parties, would have required stores to disclose the total cost of ownership up front, on the contract, on price tags, and in ads. It also would have given customers the right to reinstate an agreement after missing payments, banned confession-of-judgment clauses, wage assignments, and unlimited late fees, and set civil and criminal penalties for violations. It also would have preempted state laws that treat these deals as consumer credit requiring an annual-percentage-rate disclosure, and limited the liability of companies that buy rent-to-own contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that use rent-to-own contracts, roughly 2.3 million a year according to the bill's own findings, would gain the right to see the total cost to own an item before signing, a written total-cost figure on the contract and on store price tags, the right to reinstate a lapsed agreement within days of a missed payment (or up to 60-120 days if they had paid half or more of the total), protection against paying more than fair market value if the item is lost or destroyed, and a ban on confessions of judgment, wage assignments, waivers of legal claims, home entry without consent, and stacked late fees. The bill would also give customers one year after the last payment to sue over violations, and let the FTC and state attorneys general act against merchants with a pattern of violations.

how_it_helps.text: Requires merchants to disclose, in plain boldface terms at the top of the contract, the cash price of the item, the number and amount of payments, and the total cost to own it.
Gives customers the right to reinstate a lapsed agreement within days of a missed payment, or up to 60-120 days after surrendering the item, without losing credit toward ownership.

Bans contract terms that harm consumers in court and collections: confession-of-judgment clauses, negotiable instruments, wage assignments, waiver of legal claims, home entry without consent, and stacking of late fees.

Requires store price tags and advertisements to state the total rental-purchase cost, and allows the FTC, state attorneys general, and consumers to sue over violations, with criminal penalties for willful false disclosure.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own merchants would bear the cost of new disclosure forms, price-tag and advertising requirements, reinstatement rights, and liability for violations, including civil damages and criminal penalties for willful false disclosure. Consumers would bear a cost too, in states with stronger laws: the bill would override any state rule that treats rent-to-own as credit or requires disclosure of an annual percentage rate, so customers in those states could lose their most revealing price information. Companies that buy rent-to-own contracts would gain liability limits, but merchants assigning contracts would remain liable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rent-to-own merchants; consumers in stricter states

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state laws that regulate rent-to-own as consumer credit and specifically override any state requirement to disclose a percentage rate, so consumers in states with stricter laws could lose the ability to see the true annual cost of the deal.

Liability is limited: lawsuits against companies that buy rent-to-own contracts are allowed only for violations visible on the face of the agreement, and the consumer's signed acknowledgment of receiving disclosures counts as conclusive proof that disclosure was made, making it harder to prove a violation later.
The bill focuses on disclosure and contract terms but does not cap the total price of a rent-to-own transaction; a customer could still be shown the full total and pay many times the cash price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given rent-to-own customers real, concrete rights: a clearly stated total price before they sign, the right to reinstate after missing payments, and bans on confession-of-judgment clauses, wage assignments, and unlimited late fees. Those are genuine gains for households that often do not know they will pay two to three times the cash price. The serious drawback is the trade built into it: a federal framework that legitimizes rent-to-own as a lease rather than credit, preempts state laws that require disclosing an annual percentage rate, limits assignee liability, and treats a customer's signed acknowledgment as conclusive proof that disclosures were made. In states with stronger laws, consumers could come out worse off. An honest assessment is that the bill traded a federal floor of protections for a federal ceiling that caps consumer rights and entrenches the industry's structure.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced in April 2003, and the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 10, 2003, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote during the rest of the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005.
The bill drew 27 cosponsors, 13 Democrats and 14 Republicans, yet bipartisan support never translated into committee action.

The bill would have given rent-to-own customers the right to see the total cost of ownership before signing, reinstatement rights after missed payments, and bans on confessions of judgment, wage assignments, and unlimited late fees.

The same bill would have preempted state laws that treat rent-to-own as consumer credit and require disclosure of an annual percentage rate, and would have limited the liability of companies that buy rent-to-own contracts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own merchants came out ahead: they continued operating under a state-by-state patchwork with no federal total-cost disclosure requirement and no federal reinstatement rights for customers, and states that wanted to require rate disclosure could still do so, but the roughly 2.3 million households a year using these contracts got none of the federal protections the bill offered.

for.name: Mary Landrieu
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 10, 2003, joined by seven original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Richard Shelby
for.role: Chairman of the Senate Banking Committee; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor of the bill, whose fate then rested with the committee he chaired.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral for the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the 21 months after it was referred, leaving it to die when the 108th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly split across party lines, 13 Democratic and 14 Republican cosponsors, and no opposition ever surfaced on the record; the bill died from committee inaction, not a party fight.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed real disclosure and contract rules on rent-to-own stores, but it also would have written the industry's lease-based model into federal law and preempted state laws that treat the transactions as high-cost credit requiring an APR disclosure. Its revenue comes from customers who pay far more over time than the item's cash price, so the industry's core interest runs against the strongest consumer protection even while it accepted the disclosure rules.

industries.industry: Finance companies and assignees that buy rent-to-own contracts
industries.note: The bill limits their liability to violations visible on the face of the agreement and makes the customer's signed acknowledgment conclusive proof that disclosures were made, reducing the risk of lawsuits over contracts they purchased.
